how-to-help-a-child-control-anger:
Anger is not the problem to be removed. It is the signal that something has exceeded what a child can currently manage, and a child who never showed it would be a child suppressing something rather than a child who is fine.

What can be changed is what they do with it, and that divides cleanly into three different jobs.

Before: reducing how often it fires

Most anger is a threshold problem. The same child, well slept and fed, absorbs an annoyance that would have flattened them an hour earlier.

So the first work is unglamorous: sleep, food, and the number of demands stacked into the difficult parts of the day. Households that reduce anger usually do it here rather than in the moment.

The second is warning. A great deal of childhood anger is about being stopped without notice, which is why transitions produce more of it than anything else.

During: what actually helps

Very little that is verbal. A furious child has limited access to reasoning, so explaining, negotiating and reminding all extend the episode.

Fewer words. "I am here." Then nothing.

Lower your body. Sitting rather than standing over them changes the whole encounter.

Physical outlets if they want them. Pushing against a wall, squeezing something, stamping, running. Anger is physical and it wants somewhere to go.

Hold the limit. The feeling is allowed and the behaviour may not be. Giving way mid-rage resolves today and guarantees tomorrow.

Do not require calm before connection. "Come back when you can speak nicely" asks for the thing they have temporarily lost.

After: the part that actually teaches

Ten minutes later, briefly, when they can think.

Name what happened without a verdict. Ask what they noticed in their body just before, which builds the self-awareness that eventually gives them a warning. Agree one thing to try next time, and make it a physical action rather than an instruction to feel differently.

Then repair whatever needs repairing, and move on. Long post-mortems teach a child that anger buys an hour of intense attention.

The reframe worth holding

An angry child is usually a child who cannot yet do something, not a child who will not. Frustration, injustice, being overwhelmed, being interrupted mid-thought: these are the ordinary causes, and each has a different answer.

Asking what this anger is about is more productive than asking how to stop it.

When to seek help

Anger that is escalating rather than easing across months, that puts anybody at risk, that appears at school as well as home, or that comes with a child who seems generally unhappy rather than occasionally furious.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
why-is-my-child-angry-all-the-time:
Persistent anger, as opposed to occasional fury, almost always has a load underneath it. The useful work is finding the load, and there are six common ones.

One: they are not sleeping enough

The most common and least suspected. Short sleep in children presents as irritability and a short fuse rather than as tiredness. An hour short across a week is enough to change a child noticeably.

Count the actual hours honestly for a week before looking anywhere else.

Two: something at school

Anger at home is frequently the overflow of a day spent holding it together elsewhere. A child who is struggling academically, or socially, or with one particular adult, often behaves impeccably there and detonates in the car.

That pattern, fine at school and furious at home, is a specific clue rather than a contradiction.

Three: they cannot do something everyone expects them to do

Reading, writing, keeping up, sitting still. A child failing repeatedly at something visible carries a constant low humiliation, and humiliation converts to anger more readily than to sadness.

This is worth taking seriously because it is fixable and because the anger stops when the underlying difficulty is addressed.

Four: sensory load

Noise, crowding, clothing, lights, transitions. Some children are running near their limit all day in environments that others barely notice, and arrive home with nothing left.

Five: something changed

A move, a new sibling, a separation, a bereavement, a friend leaving, an adult in the house who is unwell or unhappy. Children rarely name these and frequently express them as anger, sometimes months later.

Worth asking directly, once, calmly, and then leaving the door open rather than pressing.

Six: it works

The one parents least like considering. If anger reliably ends demands, produces attention, or gets a decision reversed, it is being reinforced. This is not manipulation in any cynical sense; it is a child using what functions.

The fix is not punishment. It is making the calm route work better: responding readily to a request made calmly, and holding limits steadily when it is not.

How to work it out

Keep a rough note for two weeks. When does it happen, what preceded it, what ended it. Patterns emerge quickly and are usually invisible without the note, because memory attends to the worst episodes rather than the common ones.

Most families find their answer in sleep, school or an unnamed difficulty.

When to ask for help

Anger present across settings for months, getting worse rather than better, involving risk to anybody, or in a child who seems flat and unhappy underneath it. Persistent irritability in children can be a presentation of low mood, and it is worth somebody looking properly.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
how-to-handle-tantrums-in-children:
A tantrum is a nervous system past its limit, not a negotiation. Almost every mistake made during one follows from treating it as the second thing.

Why reasoning fails

A child in full distress has limited access to the parts of the brain that hold reasoning and impulse control. Explaining, bargaining and asking them to use their words are all requests for a capacity that is temporarily offline.

This is why the same sentence that works at four o'clock is useless at half past five, and why parents conclude their child is being deliberately obtuse.

What to do, in order

Make it safe. Move furniture, move them off the road, stay near. That is the whole of the first job.

Say almost nothing. One short sentence at most. "I am here." Then wait. Most of what adults say in the first minute lengthens the episode.

Lower yourself. Sit down. Standing over a screaming child keeps both bodies in a confrontation.

Stay. Nearby, unhurried, not looming and not leaving. Presence does more than words. Some children want contact and some cannot bear it during; follow what they show you.

Do not change the answer. Giving in mid-tantrum ends this one and demonstrates exactly what a tantrum achieves.

Do not teach yet. The lesson lands afterwards, briefly.

Your own state is the variable

Staying calm is a physical skill rather than a personality trait. Breathe out longer than you breathe in, unclench something, stop talking. A parent who escalates guarantees a longer episode, and a parent who stays steady shortens it without doing anything else.

Most of that is decided before the tantrum starts, by whether you are tired, hungry, late or already frayed.

In public

The same, plus ignoring the audience, which is the hard part. If you can move somewhere quieter, do. If not, proceed exactly as you would at home. The cost of abandoning your approach because strangers are watching is paid over the following weeks.

Afterwards

Keep it short. A brief naming of what happened, a repair if something needs repairing, and then genuinely move on. Long discussions afterwards teach a child that a tantrum buys an hour of intense parental attention.

No punishment for the tantrum itself. Consequences for what was done during it, if something was, are reasonable.

Reducing how often they happen

Almost entirely upstream: sleep, food, warning before transitions, fewer stacked demands in the difficult hours, and more genuine choices in the day so that a child has somewhere legitimate to exercise a will.

When to ask

Tantrums that are frequent and long past about five, that involve significant risk, or that appear in a child who is generally unhappy rather than occasionally overwhelmed.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
how-to-help-an-overwhelmed-child-calm-do:
Almost everything that works is physical, and almost everything that works happens before any conversation. That order is the whole of it.

What overwhelmed means

A nervous system taking in more than it can process: noise, people, demands, transitions, or simply a day with too much in it. What comes out is disorganised rather than defiant. More movement and less control, or a sudden shutdown.

It is not naughtiness, it is not quite tiredness, and it does not respond to instruction.

First, reduce the input

This is the intervention. Everything else is secondary.

Somewhere quieter and darker. Fewer people. No questions, no explaining, no problem-solving. If you can leave the place entirely, leave.

Say less than feels natural. Questions are more input. "Come with me" and a hand is enough.

Then, deep pressure

The most reliable physical route down, and the least known.

A firm hug, being squashed under cushions, a heavy blanket, pushing against a wall, carrying something heavy, squeezing something. Input from muscles and joints is calming in a way that light touch is not, which is why a firm hug settles a child and a gentle one sometimes does not.

Follow what they show you. Some children cannot bear contact when overwhelmed and need space plus something heavy to push against instead.

Then, slow the breathing

Not by instructing them, which rarely works. By doing it audibly yourself and letting them fall into it, or by using something that forces a long out-breath: blowing bubbles, blowing a pinwheel, drinking through a straw.

The long out-breath is the part that matters. A deep breath in on its own does very little.

Then wait

Ten to twenty minutes with nothing asked of them. This is the step most often skipped, and skipping it is why the calm does not hold.

Only then, words

And briefly. Name what happened, repair anything that needs repairing, move on.

Build the kit in advance

Decide with your child, on a calm day, what helps. A specific blanket, a particular place in the house, headphones, a bottle of water, something to squeeze. A plan made in calm conditions is available in difficult ones; a plan invented mid-crisis is not.

Preventing it

Recovery time built into busy days rather than a second event added to a full one. Leaving the party before the point at which it usually goes wrong. The day after a big day kept deliberately empty. And sleep, which is the largest background variable in how much any child can absorb.

If a child is regularly overwhelmed by ordinary environments and it is limiting what the family can do, that is worth raising with someone who can observe them directly.
